title: ShipReel
pitch: Your AI agent edits video inside the browser tab. Say "cut this to 60 seconds" and it does — trimming dead air, syncing footage to what you actually said. Nothing ever uploads.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent edits video inside the browser tab. Say "cut this to 60 seconds" and it does — trimming dead air, syncing footage to what you actually said. Nothing ever uploads. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ShipReel Inspiration Every demo video starts the same way: a raw voiceover, a few screen recordings, and forty minutes of dragging clip edges around. The work isn't really creative. It's finding the twenty-three places where I paused, trimming each one, then hunting for the moment I said “here is the terminal” so I can put the terminal footage there. That is exactly the kind of tedious, constraint-satisfying work an agent should do. But most AI video editors solve it by moving your footage to a server. For a screen recording of an unreleased product, that can be a non-starter. WebMCP changes the shape of the problem. The agent doesn't need your files — it needs your editor. What it does ShipReel is a video studio that an agent can drive through WebMCP while I stay in control. I can set a target runtime and give the agent a goal such as: “Cut this down to 60 seconds and put the terminal recording where I talk about the terminal.” The agent can inspect the timeline, detect dead air, search the transcript, place relevant footage, trim clips, add zooms, and optimize the edit until it fits the runtime budget. In a test run, a single optimize_duration call took the bundled 108.7-second edit to the 60-second target . Every action appears in an Agent Activity panel in plain English: “Removed 26.4s of dead air” “Dropped 4 lines of narration — 20.3s” “Found "Here is the terminal" in the narration at 17.4s” “Placed the terminal recording at 17.4s” The underlying WebMCP tool name and arguments remain visible underneath as evidence. My own manual edits appear in the same activity feed, so a drag I make by hand and a cut made by the agent become one shared history. The footage doesn't have to be the bundled kind. Dropping a screen recording onto the timeline adds it to the project — nothing uploads, and it takes exactly the same path as the bundled clips, so every tool treats it identically. The clip id comes from the filename, so login-flow.mov lets me say, “put the login flow clip at 45 seconds.” The agent sees the imported footage on its next get_project_state , the same way it sees a manual edit. Why this had to be WebMCP, not a backend MCP server Most agent integrations can use a remote MCP server. This one is different. The media is held in page memory. HTMLVideoElement decodes video, Canvas composites the preview, the Web Audio graph handles audio, and encoding uses MediaRecorder — all inside the tab. There is no remote media service that needs to own the edit. A backend MCP server would not naturally have access to the live timeline state, decoded audio, or the rendered frame the user is looking at. The clearest example is preview_at . preview_at does not change the edit. It moves the user's playhead so the agent can show the human exactly what it is referring to. Over a backend-only protocol, that tool has little meaning. With WebMCP, the agent can operate on the same live interface the human is watching. During testing inside ChatGPT's built-in browser, the agent independently called preview_at at 17.4 seconds to show the clip it had placed. I had not explicitly asked it to preview that timestamp. That was the point where the premise stopped being an architectural argument and became a visible demonstration. The agent is a guest in the editor, not the other way round. How I built it ShipReel is built with React, TypeScript, Zustand, Tailwind and Vite. The editing engine is written from scratch without a video-editing library. Ripple delete across tracks remove_ranges accepts an array of time spans and closes all the gaps in one operation, keeping narration and footage aligned. Instead of making the agent issue a separate request for every silent section, it can remove a whole set of ranges in a single tool call. Silence detection find_silences analyzes the decoded audio with windowed RMS and derives a threshold from the recording itself. The bundled voiceover contains 28.3 seconds of detected dead air . Runtime optimization optimize_duration is the high-level tool. It first reclaims low-cost time such as silence, then escalates to progressively more expensive edits such as filler removal and whole-sentence removal until the edit fits the requested runtime. It protects the opening sentence from becoming a candidate because saving a few seconds is not worth destroying the hook. When multiple lines could close the remaining gap, the optimizer prefers the shortest sufficient line, avoiding unnecessary loss of narration. Real-time in-tab export The export path drives the same player/compositor used for preview and captures its canvas and audio graph with MediaRecorder . The render clock runs in a Worker instead of relying on requestAnimationFrame , so rendering is not tied directly to the visible frame loop. Fourteen WebMCP tools Fourteen tools are available across two states. At boot — 7 tools: get_project_state search_transcript find_silences optimize_duration remove_ranges place_clip preview_at After footage is present — 7 additional tools: trim_clip move_clip set_clip_speed add_zoom remove_clip get_export_status export_video The clip-editing tools register only when there is footage on the video track, so the agent is not offered actions that are meaningless in the current state. Tool descriptions are designed around one job per tool, non-overlapping responsibilities, bounded outputs, and recovery-oriented error messages. Human + agent collaboration ShipReel is not designed around replacing the human editor. The agent handles repetitive operations and constraint satisfaction. The human can still inspect the result, move clips, change timing, or intervene at any point. For example: “Preview the terminal section.” The agent can call: preview_at(17.4) I see the exact part of the edit it is referring to, decide whether the placement is good, and continue directing the work. That makes the browser itself the shared workspace between human and agent. Challenges Making “hit a target runtime” an agent problem instead of a guessing game The first version reclaimed whatever time it could and then stopped, returning candidate sentences for me to choose between. That worked, but it did not solve the actual problem. The rewrite turned runtime optimization into an iterative constraint problem: reclaim silence reclaim low-cost filler remove whole sentences only when necessary stop immediately when the target is satisfied A subtle selection detail mattered. When multiple lines could close the remaining gap, the optimizer chooses the shortest sufficient line instead of deleting more content than necessary. That turned a 60-second target from a rough approximation into a controlled optimization process. A silence-detection bug I only found by writing evals find_silences originally truncated its returned list at a response cap while still reporting the full count. That meant an agent could remove only the ranges it received and incorrectly believe the job was complete. I changed the tool to make truncation explicit and to instruct the agent to call again for the remaining ranges. The fix came from an agent-level evaluation, not from a traditional unit test. Layout that only broke where it mattered The preview frame used an aspect-ratio box with a max-height , which behaved correctly at desktop widths but failed inside the narrower layout used by ChatGPT's browser pane. I found it in a responsive audit at 900×800 — and then realised ChatGPT's browser pane renders below that same breakpoint, so it would have hit exactly there. The content-sized grid row allowed the preview to grow beyond its intended slot and paint over the timeline. What I learned Write evals for the tool surface, not just the code I built a 17-task evaluation suite that drives real Chrome with WebMCP enabled and executes the same sequences a competent agent would perform. The suite caught real bugs that ordinary unit tests did not expose. It also runs against the production deployment, so I can validate the same behavior that a judge will see. The seventeenth task covers bring-your-own-media end to end: a screen recording goes through the real file input, the agent is told about it, the footage is placed by name, and the resulting canvas is verified to remain untainted — an important check because imported media can otherwise silently break browser export. Tool design is product design The most useful WebMCP decision was adding the high-level optimize_duration tool. Without it, an agent has to manually orchestrate silence detection, transcript search, filler removal and sentence selection across many calls.
